attorney_selection_framework.title: How to evaluate a personal injury lawyer in Fargo, North Dakota
attorney_selection_framework.case_type_specialization: In Fargo, start by matching the lawyer to the injury and liability pattern: car accident, truck accident, slip and fall, pedestrian or bicycle injury, catastrophic injury, wrongful death, or an uninsured/underinsured motorist issue. Do not treat broad advertising as proof of case-type fit.
attorney_selection_framework.contingency_terms: For North Dakota personal injury consultations, ask for the contingency percentage, whether it changes after filing or trial preparation, how case expenses are advanced or deducted, and how medical liens or reimbursements affect net recovery. This is a review checklist, not a statement of a fixed state fee rule.
attorney_selection_framework.trial_readiness: Ask whether the firm files suit when negotiation stalls, who handles litigation, whether trial counsel is involved, and whether a case like yours might be referred out. Trial readiness matters when fault, injury severity, or insurer valuation is disputed in Fargo.
attorney_selection_framework.reviews_and_reputation: Use reviews as process signals, not rankings. Look for patterns around communication, case updates, fee transparency, staff handoff, and whether people understood next steps. Then verify attorney status through the official North Dakota resource when available.
attorney_selection_framework.attorney_verification: For North Dakota, use the official attorney registration, bar, or disciplinary resource before relying on a directory listing. Confirm the lawyer's current status and any public discipline through the official state source when available.
attorney_selection_framework.deadline_caveat: Deadlines, notice rules, and filing requirements can vary by claim type and defendant in North Dakota. Verify timing directly with a qualified lawyer or official source before waiting on records, insurer calls, or settlement discussions.
attorney_selection_framework.directory_use_note: Use the Fargo directory as a neutral starting list, not as a ranking or endorsement. Compare each firm against the same case-fit, fee, trial-readiness, review, and verification questions before contacting anyone.
attorney_selection_framework.local_context_note: For Fargo, keep the comparison practical: case type fit, written contingency terms, who handles the file, trial-readiness posture, and review patterns that describe communication rather than popularity.
attorney_selection_framework.educational_boundary: Educational only. Not legal advice. No attorney-client relationship, endorsement, ranking, or guarantee is created.

payment_options: Ask whether the fee is contingency-based, whether litigation expenses are advanced, and whether costs come out before or after the fee calculation.

wait_time_notes: Speed matters most at the beginning because evidence, treatment records, scene photos, and insurance notices can get harder to organize later.
A same-day callback is less important than getting clear preservation steps and a real screening conversation.
availability_notes: Availability should be judged by whether the team can review the facts quickly and tell you what to gather next, not just by how fast intake answers the phone.
Ask whether weekends, after-hours intake, bilingual staff, or remote consultation options are available if timing is urgent.

case_screening_notes: Ask what facts, treatment records, photos, witnesses, or insurance details make a Fargo consultation productive instead of generic.
A strong screening call should explain what is missing, what should be preserved now, and what could weaken the claim if ignored.
Do not treat marketing confidence as proof of case fit; compare how clearly each firm explains liability, damages, and next steps.
fee_structure_notes: For North Dakota personal injury consultations, ask for the contingency percentage, whether it changes after filing or trial preparation, how case expenses are advanced or deducted, and how medical liens or reimbursements affect net recovery. This is a review checklist, not a statement of a fixed state fee rule.
Ask whether case costs are advanced, when they are deducted, how liens or reimbursements are handled, and what the net-recovery conversation sounds like before you sign.
If two firms quote a similar contingency percentage, the more useful comparison is usually how clearly they explain expenses, deductions, and settlement math.
trial_readiness_notes: Ask who will own the file day to day, when a claim is escalated toward filing, and what trial preparation actually looks like if the insurer refuses to negotiate fairly in Fargo.
Trial posture matters because insurers price risk differently when they believe a firm can prove damages, preserve evidence, and move a case through litigation.
A useful comparison question is whether the firm can explain negotiation strategy, filing thresholds, and communication expectations without rushing you to sign.
